newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Ross sees start to Israel-PLO security links.
newsitem.headline: Ross sees start to Israel-PLO security links.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross said on Tuesday that Israel and the Palestinians had made a start to restoring security cooperation.
"We have a beginning, we have a step in the right direction but we need to see results," Ross said after his third meeting in as many days with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"What we'll be looking for, what we'll be watching is in fact how this process develops and whether or not it produces results," he told reporters.
Ross, who has brought Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security experts together during his mission, said he expected to end his visit on Wednesday.
He flew to the region at the weekend after a double suicide bombing by Moslem militants in Jerusalem's main Jewish market threatened to shatter already fragile Israeli-Palestinian ties.

The difficulty of his task was driven home in the West Bank town of Nablus, where around 10,000 Palestinians marched in protest against U.S. and Israeli pressure on Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to crack down on the militants.
Witnesses said masked youths burned a dummy of Ross dressed as an ultra-Orthodox Jew holding a doll resembling Netanyahu.
"This is a message to Ross. Stop U.S. bias towards Israel and stop pressuring the Palestinian Authority to make concessions to Israel," one protester said.

Also in Nablus, a Palestinian military court sentenced one member of Arafat's presidential guard to death and two other guards to long prison sentences on Tuesday for treason and collaboration with Israel, witnesses said.
The three were arrested last month and charged with terrorising, abducting and killing Palestinians on orders from a "foreign country".

Netanyahu, who flies to Jordan on Wednesday for talks with King Hussein on the crisis in the peace process, has accused Arafat of doing "damn all" to smash what he says is a "terrorist infrastructure" operating from Palestinian self-rule areas.
"The goal is not holding these (security) meetings but getting real results from these meetings. These things will be tested in the coming days, the coming weeks," he said.

He says real security cooperation from Arafat must come before any resumption of peace talks and before any significant lifting of sanctions he has slapped on Palestinian self-rule areas since the July 30 bombing.

Jordan said King Hussein, the first Arab leader to meet the Israeli leader since the attack, would urge Netanyahu to ease the sanctions, which include a closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, at their summit in the Red Sea resort of Aqaba.
"There has been some relaxation of some of the measures...But we are not satisfied," Jordanian Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawnah told Reuters in Amman. "Many of the steps were totally unjustified."
Tarawnah said Israel should also revoke a freeze on the transfer of customs revenues to the Palestinian Authority, which he said was "totally illegal".

Arafat, who was to meet Ross in the West Bank town of Ramallah later on Tuesday, has insisted he is making a "100 percent effort" on security and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to weaken his legitimacy.
The two bombers, who killed 14 other people in their attack, have not yet been identified nor has a claim of responsibility from the Moslem militant group Hamas been fully authenticated.

Ross has made clear throughout his mission that his focus is on security, a stance supported by Israel, but Palestinian officials have countered that political progress must accompany improved intelligence sharing.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks had already been in stalemate well before the bombing over a Jewish settlement Israel began building in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
Palestinians want construction halted, an end to Israel's demolition of Palestinian houses and land confiscations and a lifting of Netanyahu's punitive measures.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, eager to bring the sides into accelerated final peace talks, is expected to make her first visit to the region late this month if she deems enough progress has been made on security cooperation.
